column2: The start screen now lets you choose between the Map editor and the Mod editor; the top bar has a Mod editor button too.
The Mod editor has its own tutorial, Ctrl+S to pack and Ctrl+Z to undo; on phones its top bar scrolls sideways.
READMEs in Traditional Chinese, Japanese, Russian and Spanish.

Open a Mod to browse its units, edit values, check problems and pack it again. It works much like the map editor: Ctrl+S saves (packs), Ctrl+Z undoes.
This is Terrain mode. Pick a terrain on the right (at the bottom on phones), for example Shallow water.
Press and drag on the map to paint. Notice that edges get transitions automatically (beach, shallows) — no hand-placing tiles.
Made a mistake? Tap Undo. On a computer press Ctrl+Z; on a phone a two-finger tap also works.
Versus maps are usually symmetric. Under “Symmetry” pick Left-right, then paint again — the other half is painted at the same time.
Switch to Items mode, then tap the map once to place a resource pool.
Switch to Units mode and tap the map once to place a spawn (command center + 2 builders). Team numbers are assigned in order.
Press Playable? to check: missing map_info, spawns on water, crowded resource pools… it tells you, and many problems can be fixed in one tap.
Finally Save. The small arrow next to it also offers “Save to game folder”, so you can go straight into the game.
Pick the Marquee tool (shortcut M).
Drag a box on the map to select an area.
A bar appears below: copy, cut, flip, rotate. Tap Copy, then Paste.
After selecting, tap “Save stamp”: it appears in the Stamps panel on the right and can be placed with one tap later. The panel also has built-in bases, lakes, shallows and more.
Switch to Triggers mode. Triggers are the map's rules: when something happens, then do something.
The quickest way is a template. Tap City capture, give it a name, then tap the city's position on the map.
Tap “Logic graph” to see how all triggers connect: green lines are “activate”, red dashed lines are “deactivate”. Afterwards press “Playable?” to check.
Generate mode works on the whole map: random generation, image to map, proportional scaling, whole-map mirroring and canvas resize.

Image to map: pick an image, the main colours are found automatically, you decide which terrain each becomes and in what proportion; generate when the preview looks right, then fine-tune piece by piece.
Proportional scaling: when the map is doubled, terrain is re-laid automatically, spawns and resource pools move with it, and more pools can be added by area.
Switch to Terrain mode and tap Auto detail at the top right of the panel (also in the menu “Generate → Auto detail”).
First pick a style preset, such as “Lakeside meadow”. A preset is a combination of modifiers; the right side lists what it does.
Each modifier can be tuned: how many trees, how wide the beach, how the river bends. Preview only looks; press Apply when happy.
Look at the result — spawns and resource pools are kept clear of trees automatically. If you don't like it, Ctrl+Z; the whole application is one step.
Open the menu “Map → Balance report” to see each team's nearest resource pool, how many are within 30 cells, and territory size.
Rows with a big gap turn yellow. Auto balance moves the disadvantaged team's pools toward their spawn or adds a new one, and the whole change is one undo step.
Now try “Map → Chokepoints”: it computes how far each team has to walk to the other and marks narrow passes. Capture-point maps depend on this.
Always press Playable? before publishing. It lists everything that can be fixed in one tap — pools in water, spawns too close, triggers referring to names that don't exist…
Check logic before going into the game: menu “Triggers → Trigger simulator”; drag the timeline to see when each one fires and how many times.
For a cover image use “File → Export screenshot”: it renders a high-resolution PNG from the real tiles, with optional grid and resource pool markers.
Finally save the .tmx and put it in the game's maps folder. To post it on the workshop use “File → Workshop package”: cover, description and changelog in one package.
Lesson 8: Edit a Mod unit and pack it
Mod editor: create, edit values, check, pack into .rwmod
This is the Mod editor. Tap New Mod to get a ready-made sample unit. To edit your own Mod, tap “Open” and load a .rwmod or zip.
I already have it open
On the left is the unit list; each row shows price, health and speed. Tap a unit.
On the right is the form: the ⓘ next to each field explains what the value does. Try changing the price or health.
A mistake is fine: tap ↶ to undo (Ctrl+Z on a computer). Tap “Source” to see the raw file.
Before packing, tap Check: missing images, projectiles that don't exist, odd values… all listed.
Finally tap Pack .rwmod (Ctrl+S on a computer) and put it in the game's mods folder.
Not now
Lesson 9: The Mod toolbox
Scale, variants, comparison, share codes, publish package, plus autosave and trash
Open or create a Mod first, then tap Tools. They are grouped by purpose: make units, bulk edit, compare and balance, share and publish.
I see it
Scale values / Generate variants: make a stronger or weaker version in one go. Comparison table / Battle simulation: see which unit wins (an estimate, for reference only).
Unit share code: pack a unit into a line of text; a friend pastes it to import. Publish package: pre-check, version number and changelog packed into one zip.
Every change is autosaved and can be recovered after a refresh; deleted units can be found again in the Trash.
At any time tap the ? next to a tool for help, or press Ctrl+K (on a phone: top-left menu → Search) to find a feature by name.
